questions.stem: A sperm cell has a long tail and many mitochondria. How do these suit its function?
options: The tail digests the egg membrane and the mitochondria store nutrients
The tail anchors the sperm to the uterus and the mitochondria make hormones
The tail carries the genetic material and the mitochondria trigger division
The tail propels the sperm and the mitochondria supply the ATP for movement
questions.explanation: A sperm's job is to travel to the egg, so it needs a motile tail and a concentrated energy supply; mitochondria release ATP by cellular respiration to drive the flagellum. The option about digesting the egg membrane confuses the flagellum with the acrosome, the enzyme-filled cap at the sperm's head that does break down the egg's outer layers. Remember: head carries DNA and acrosome, midpiece carries mitochondria, tail provides movement.

questions.stem: In a flowering plant, which structure produces pollen and which structure receives it?
options: The ovary produces pollen; the style receives it
The filament produces pollen; the ovule receives it
The anther produces pollen; the stigma receives it
The stigma produces pollen; the anther receives it
questions.explanation: The anther, held up by the filament, is the male part where pollen grains form, and the sticky stigma at the top of the style is the female surface that catches pollen. Swapping stigma and anther is the most common error; the cue is that the stigma is sticky or feathery for catching pollen, while anthers are the sacs that split open to release it. The ovary and ovules sit at the base and hold the female gametes, not pollen.

questions.stem: What is asexual reproduction?
options: One parent produces genetically identical offspring, no gametes
Two parents each contribute gametes, but offspring resemble one
One parent produces gametes that develop unfertilised
Two identical parents fuse cells, giving new gene mixes
questions.explanation: Asexual reproduction involves a single parent and mitosis, so offspring are clones apart from rare mutations. The option about gametes developing without fertilisation describes a special case sometimes discussed separately, but it wrongly claims varied offspring arise as the general rule of asexual reproduction, and standard asexual reproduction does not involve gametes at all. The defining cue is: no gamete fusion, one parent, genetically identical offspring.

questions.stem: Strawberry plants spread by runners, producing new plants that are genetically identical to the parent. A new fungal disease that these plants have no resistance to arrives in the area. What is the most likely outcome?
options: The plants will switch permanently to sexual reproduction as soon as the disease appears
Almost the whole population is vulnerable, because there is little genetic variation for resistance
The plants will rapidly evolve resistance, because runners produce many new plants quickly
Only the parent plant will die, because runner offspring are younger and therefore stronger
questions.explanation: Asexual reproduction produces clones, so if the parent lacks a resistance allele none of the offspring have one, and a single pathogen can wipe out the whole stand. The option about rapidly evolving resistance is tempting because fast reproduction does matter, but evolution needs variation to select from, and cloning supplies almost none. Speed of reproduction and variety of genotypes are two different advantages.

questions.stem: What happens after a pollen grain lands on a compatible stigma?
options: A pollen tube grows down the style so a male nucleus can reach the ovule
The grain is drawn down the style and develops directly into a seed
The stigma releases male nuclei that travel up into the anther
The grain divides on the stigma, and the embryo is pushed into the ovary
questions.explanation: Pollen cannot swim, so it grows a tube through the style as a delivery route for the male nucleus to reach the ovule, where fertilisation occurs and a seed then forms. The option saying the grain itself becomes a seed is tempting because pollen and seeds are both small and dry, but a seed is a fertilised ovule containing an embryo, not a transported pollen grain. Cue: pollen delivers a nucleus; the ovule supplies the egg cell and becomes the seed.

questions.stem: Human testes are held in the scrotum, outside the main body cavity. What is the functional reason for this arrangement?
options: Sperm production works best at a temperature slightly below normal core body temperature
Sperm must be stored in dry air outside the body before they can become motile
The position lets sperm absorb oxygen directly through the scrotal skin from the surroundings
Sperm cells would be destroyed by the acidity of the abdominal cavity if the testes were internal
questions.explanation: Sperm formation is temperature-sensitive and proceeds properly a couple of degrees below core body temperature, which the external scrotum provides. The suggestion that sperm need dry air is wrong: sperm are always kept in fluid, and mature in the epididymis inside the scrotum, never exposed to air. Link structure to function by asking what condition the tissue needs — here it is cooling.

questions.stem: A frog releases thousands of eggs into a pond and the male sheds sperm over them; a horse produces one offspring at a time and fertilisation is internal. Which comparison is correct?
options: External fertilisation produces far more gametes because a much smaller proportion of them ever meet and survive
External fertilisation produces more offspring because each frog egg reliably develops into more than one tadpole
Internal fertilisation produces fewer offspring because horse sperm cannot swim to reach the egg
Internal fertilisation produces fewer offspring because the eggs of mammals cannot be fertilised more than once
questions.explanation: When gametes are released into open water, most sperm never reach an egg and most young are eaten or die, so high numbers compensate for low survival; internal fertilisation and parental care raise the survival chance of each offspring, so fewer are needed. The claim that each frog egg makes several tadpoles is simply false — one fertilised egg gives one tadpole. The cue is survival rate, not egg-splitting.

questions.stem: A gardener takes cuttings from one prize-winning rose bush and roots them to make 50 new plants. Which statement about these new plants is correct?
options: They are genetically identical to the parent, so the desirable flower traits are reliably reproduced
They show a mixture of the parent's traits and new ones, because rooting a cutting involves fertilisation
They are genetically identical, and so are guaranteed to be resistant to any disease that appears
They will each carry half the parent's genes, because a cutting contains only part of the parent plant
questions.explanation: Taking cuttings is asexual reproduction: the new plants come from mitosis of parent tissue only, so they are clones and reproduce the parent's traits exactly. The option adding a disease-resistance guarantee is tempting because clones do inherit the parent's resistance genes, but a clone population is uniformly vulnerable to anything the parent could not resist. Cue: identical genes means identical strengths and identical weaknesses.

questions.stem: Some sea anemones can reproduce both sexually and asexually. In a stable, unchanging rock pool where they are already well suited to conditions, what is the main advantage of the asexual pathway?
options: Offspring inherit new gene combinations, letting the population adapt faster to the stable conditions
Offspring are produced by meiosis, which is quicker than the mitosis used in sexual reproduction
Offspring are always larger at birth, because asexual young receive genes from two parents
Offspring can be produced rapidly without a mate, quickly filling space with well-suited genotypes
questions.explanation: Asexual reproduction skips finding a mate and producing gametes, so numbers build quickly, and in an environment that is not changing, copies of an already successful genotype do well. The option about new gene combinations describes the advantage of sexual reproduction, and in any case variation is of least value when conditions are stable. Cue: variation pays off when the environment changes; speed and certainty pay off when it does not.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly defines fertilisation?
options: The lining of the uterus thickens so that a developing embryo can attach to it
The nucleus of a male gamete fuses with the nucleus of a female gamete to form a zygote
A gamete divides into two identical cells that then grow into an embryo
Pollen or sperm is transferred to the female reproductive structure of the same species
questions.explanation: Fertilisation is specifically the fusion of two gametes, so that one cell with a full set of chromosomes, the zygote, is produced. The transfer of pollen or sperm is tempting but that describes pollination or mating, which brings the gametes close together without any fusion occurring. Remember: transfer gets the gametes to the same place, fertilisation is the fusion itself.

questions.stem: Which statement about the human ovaries is correct?
options: They produce ova and release one roughly every month into the oviduct
They produce ova and hold them until an embryo is ready to implant
They receive ova from the uterus and store them until fertilisation occurs
They produce the fluid that carries ova along towards the uterus lining
questions.explanation: The ovaries are the female gonads: they contain the developing egg cells and release a mature ovum at ovulation, usually about once a month, into the funnel of the oviduct. The option saying they hold ova until an embryo implants is wrong because implantation happens in the uterus lining, well after the egg has left the ovary. Track the order: ovary, oviduct (where fertilisation happens), then uterus.

questions.stem: After successful fertilisation in a flowering plant such as an apple tree, what happens to the ovule and the ovary?
options: The ovary becomes the seed and the ovule develops into the fleshy fruit around it
The ovule becomes the fruit and the ovary dies back once the petals have fallen
The ovule and ovary both become seeds, while the stigma swells into the fruit
The ovule becomes the seed and the ovary wall develops into the fruit around it
questions.explanation: Each fertilised ovule inside the ovary develops into a seed containing the embryo plant and a food store, and the surrounding ovary wall thickens into the fruit that protects and helps disperse those seeds. Swapping the two, so that the ovary becomes the seed, is the common trap; remember the ovary is the outer container, so it becomes the outer fruit. A useful cue is that an apple with several pips came from one ovary holding several ovules.

questions.stem: Grass flowers are small and dull with feathery stigmas hanging outside the flower, and they release huge amounts of very light, smooth pollen. What can you correctly conclude?
options: The grass is wind pollinated, and the light pollen means fertilisation happens without any pollen tube growing
The grass is self pollinating only, and the dull flowers show that its pollen never leaves the plant
The grass is wind pollinated, and the feathery stigma gives a large area to catch drifting pollen grains
The grass is insect pollinated, and the feathery stigma provides a landing platform for visiting insects
questions.explanation: Wind pollinated flowers invest in quantity rather than attraction: no need for bright petals, nectar or sticky sculptured pollen, but a big feathery stigma greatly increases the chance of intercepting grains carried on air currents. The insect pollination option is the tempting one, but insect pollinated flowers are typically showy and scented with sticky pollen, none of which the grass has. Whatever the pollination method, a pollen tube must still grow down the style for fertilisation to occur.

questions.stem: A human egg is large and packed with food-storing cytoplasm. How does that suit its function?
options: The cytoplasm lets the egg swim up the oviduct towards the sperm
The extra cytoplasm carries the second set of chromosomes needed by the embryo
The stored material blocks sperm from digesting through the egg coat
The stored nutrients feed the early embryo before it implants in the uterus
questions.explanation: After fertilisation the zygote divides many times while travelling to the uterus, and it has no external food supply until implantation, so the egg's cytoplasmic reserves fuel that early development. The option about swimming up the oviduct is the tempting one, but eggs are not motile — they are moved along by cilia and muscular contractions of the oviduct wall, while the sperm supplies the movement. Remember the division of labour: sperm brings mobility and DNA, egg brings DNA plus the food store.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an example of asexual reproduction?
options: An apple tree growing seeds that germinate into young trees
A frog laying spawn that a male frog then sheds sperm over
A pollen grain growing a tube down the style to reach an ovule
A potato tuber sprouting to produce several new potato plants
questions.explanation: Asexual reproduction involves one parent and no fusion of gametes, so a tuber sprouting into new plants that are genetically identical to the parent qualifies. Seeds from an apple tree are tempting because they are also produced by a plant, but seeds form only after pollen and ovule gametes fuse, which is sexual reproduction. The test is always whether two gametes combine, not whether the organism is a plant or an animal.

questions.stem: Which statement best explains why offspring produced by sexual reproduction are not identical to either parent?
options: Only the female parent's genes are passed on, but they are shuffled during pregnancy
Each offspring receives a different combination of genes from two parents' gametes
Gametes copy the parents' DNA inaccurately, so every offspring carries new errors
The offspring's genes change to suit the environment it develops and grows in
questions.explanation: Sexual reproduction mixes genetic material: a haploid gamete from each parent fuses, and each gamete carries its own combination of the parent's genes, so every offspring is genetically unique. The option about copying errors is tempting because mutations do occur, but they are rare accidents and are not the main source of the variation seen between siblings. Link variation to the shuffling and combining of two parents' genes, not to mistakes or to the environment.

questions.stem: Before ovulation, the lining of the human uterus thickens and develops a rich supply of blood vessels. How does this structure relate to its function?
options: It produces the egg cells that will be released into the oviduct each cycle
It pushes the egg along the oviduct so that sperm can reach and fertilise it
It thickens to stop more than one sperm cell entering the released egg
It can supply an implanted embryo with oxygen and nutrients from the mother's blood
questions.explanation: An embryo that implants has no food supply of its own, so a thick, well-vascularised lining allows exchange of oxygen and nutrients with the mother's blood, later through the placenta. The option about producing egg cells confuses the uterine lining with the ovary, which is where eggs mature. If the lining is not needed it breaks down and is shed during menstruation.

questions.stem: Yeast cells in a warm, sugar-rich brewing vat reproduce by budding, where a small outgrowth pinches off as a new cell. Why is this method an advantage in these conditions?
options: Each bud can choose useful features from the parent as conditions in the vat change
One parent alone can multiply rapidly, quickly filling a habitat that already suits it
The buds carry new gene combinations, so some will survive if the sugar runs out
Budding needs two parent cells, which speeds up growth compared with using gametes
questions.explanation: Asexual reproduction needs no mate and no gamete fusion, so numbers can build up very fast, which pays off where conditions are stable and the parent is already well suited. The option about new gene combinations is tempting but wrong for budding: buds are clones of the parent, so genetic variation is essentially absent. Remember the trade-off — asexual gives speed and numbers, sexual gives variation.

questions.stem: In mosses and ferns, male gametes swim through a film of water to reach the egg, but in flowering plants the male gametes are delivered by a pollen tube growing down the style. What does this difference show about structure and function?
options: Flowering plant gametes are diploid, so they are too heavy to swim and must be carried in a tube
The pollen tube exists to carry nutrients from the stigma to feed the developing seed coat
Mosses and ferns are asexual, so their swimming cells are spores rather than true gametes
The pollen tube replaces the need for external water, so flowering plants can reproduce in dry habitats
questions.explanation: Delivering male gametes inside a growing pollen tube means fertilisation no longer depends on a surface film of water, which is a key reason flowering plants succeed in dry environments. The claim that flowering plant gametes are diploid is false — gametes are haploid in all sexually reproducing organisms, and fusion restores the diploid number. Focus on the delivery problem each structure solves: swimming needs water, a tube does not.

questions.stem: A body cell of a particular animal contains 24 chromosomes. Which statement about this animal's gametes and zygote is correct?
options: Each gamete has 24 chromosomes, and the zygote formed at fertilisation has 48
Each gamete has 12 chromosomes, and the zygote also has 12 until it starts dividing
Sperm have 24 chromosomes and eggs have 12, giving a zygote with 36 chromosomes
Each gamete has 12 chromosomes, and the zygote formed at fertilisation has 24
questions.explanation: Gametes are made by meiosis and carry half the body-cell number, here 12, so that when two gametes fuse the zygote is restored to the species number of 24. The option giving gametes 24 chromosomes and a zygote of 48 is the common trap: if gametes kept the full number, the chromosome count would double every generation. Check your answer by making sure the zygote total matches the body-cell number given in the question.

questions.stem: The oviduct is lined with beating cilia and has smooth muscle in its wall. What is that for?
options: They produce the egg cells that are released each month
They supply the developing embryo with oxygen and nutrients
They thicken each month and are shed during menstruation
They move the egg along towards the uterus after ovulation
questions.explanation: The oviduct's job is transport: cilia sweep and muscular contractions push the egg (or early embryo) from the ovary towards the uterus, and fertilisation usually happens inside it. Saying the tube produces the egg cells confuses the oviduct with the ovary, which is the organ where eggs mature and are released. A useful cue is that ovaries make and release, while the oviduct only moves and hosts fertilisation.

questions.stem: A sperm head is capped by an acrosome full of enzymes. What is it for?
options: It holds a spare copy of the chromosomes if the nucleus is damaged
It digests a path through the egg's coating so the nucleus can enter
It releases energy for the tail so the sperm can swim to the egg
It carries food reserves to nourish the zygote after fertilisation
questions.explanation: Fertilisation requires the sperm to get through the layers surrounding the egg, and the acrosome's enzymes break these down so the two nuclei can fuse. The energy option is tempting because sperm do need lots of energy, but that comes from mitochondria packed into the midpiece, not the acrosome. Link the part to the job: head plus acrosome for entry, midpiece for energy, tail for movement.

questions.stem: In humans, where does fertilisation normally take place?
options: In the lining of the uterus, where implantation occurs
In the vagina, where the sperm are first deposited
In the upper part of the oviduct (fallopian tube)
In the ovary, immediately after the egg is released
questions.explanation: Sperm swim up through the uterus and meet the egg in the oviduct, and the resulting zygote then travels down to implant in the uterus lining. Choosing the uterus lining confuses fertilisation with implantation, which happens several days later once a ball of cells arrives there. Remember the order: fertilisation in the tube, implantation in the uterus.

questions.stem: A single bacterium in a warm nutrient broth divides by binary fission roughly every 20 minutes. Which statement best explains the survival advantage of this form of reproduction here?
options: One cell can rapidly build a huge population without needing a partner
Each division shuffles the genes, so the population becomes highly varied
Each new cell receives half the parent's DNA, keeping cells small and fast
Offspring are produced only when conditions worsen, saving resources
questions.explanation: Asexual reproduction needs no mate and no gamete fusion, so in favourable conditions numbers can multiply extremely quickly from a single individual. The option about shuffling genes describes sexual reproduction; binary fission copies the DNA, so offspring are genetically almost identical clones. The cue is that variation comes from sexual reproduction, while speed and independence come from asexual reproduction.

questions.stem: The placenta has a very large surface area made of finger-like villi, and these are surrounded by pools of the mother's blood. How does this structure relate to its function?
options: It produces the eggs and sperm needed for the next generation
It stores the food reserves that were originally packed into the egg cell
It speeds up exchange of oxygen and nutrients between mother and fetus
It allows the mother's and fetus's blood to mix so they share one supply
questions.explanation: A large surface area in close contact with maternal blood shortens diffusion distances and increases the rate at which oxygen, glucose and wastes can be exchanged. The mixing option is a common error: the two blood supplies stay separate, and substances pass across the thin membranes of the villi by diffusion. Look for the phrase 'blood mixing' as a warning sign, since exchange without mixing is the whole point of the placenta.

questions.stem: Pollen grains have a tough, waterproof outer wall that is often sculptured or spiky. How does this structure relate to the grain's function?
options: It absorbs water from the air so the grain can swell and burst on the stigma
It protects the male gametes from drying out while pollen is carried between flowers
It allows the grain to photosynthesise while it is being carried on the wind
It stops the grain germinating until the whole flower has been fertilised
questions.explanation: Pollen must survive a journey through air or on an animal's body, so a tough waterproof coat protects the delicate cells inside from damage and dehydration, and sculpturing helps grains stick to pollinators. The idea that the wall stops germination gets the timing backwards, since a compatible stigma triggers a pollen tube to grow out through a pore in that wall. Think of the wall as travel armour, not a switch controlling development.

questions.stem: Some gecko species are all female and reproduce by parthenogenesis, where eggs develop without fertilisation. A single gecko is blown onto a bare volcanic island. Compared with a sexually reproducing species, what is the main advantage here?
options: The offspring will show more genetic variation, so they adapt to the island faster
The offspring will each inherit half the parent's chromosomes and stay small
Reproduction will only begin once a mate of the other sex also arrives
One individual alone can found an entire breeding population on the island
questions.explanation: Asexual reproduction removes the need to find a mate, so a lone coloniser can immediately produce offspring and establish a population, which is a real advantage on isolated islands. The variation option is the trap: parthenogenetic offspring are essentially clones, so variation is low and the population is vulnerable to a new disease or environmental change. Match the advantage to the situation — asexual reproduction wins on speed and independence, sexual reproduction wins on variation.

questions.stem: Many flowering plants are self-incompatible: pollen landing on a stigma of the same plant fails to grow a pollen tube, while pollen from another plant of the species succeeds. What is the main survival benefit of this mechanism?
options: It guarantees every ovule is fertilised, increasing the number of seeds
It allows the plant to reproduce without needing pollinators or wind
It forces cross-pollination, so offspring carry a wider mix of genes
It prevents the plant wasting energy on producing pollen at all
questions.explanation: Blocking self-pollen means gametes must come from two different parents, which increases genetic variation in the seeds and improves the species' chances of surviving disease or environmental change. The 'guarantees every ovule is fertilised' option is tempting because self-pollination is convenient, but self-incompatibility actually reduces the chance of fertilisation in exchange for greater variation. The cue is that any mechanism keeping two parents involved is about variation, not about seed numbers.

questions.stem: In the human male reproductive system, which structure carries sperm from the testis towards the urethra?
options: The sperm duct (vas deferens), a muscular tube leading from the testis
The scrotum, a muscular sac that pumps sperm along to the penis
The prostate gland, a tube that channels sperm from the testis into the bladder
The seminal vesicle, a narrow duct linking the two testes to each other
questions.explanation: The sperm duct, or vas deferens, is a muscular tube whose walls contract to move sperm from the epididymis of each testis to the urethra, where fluids from glands are added. The prostate option is tempting because the prostate is a real male structure, but it is a gland that adds fluid to semen, not a transport tube, and sperm never travel into the bladder. Cue: ducts transport, glands secrete fluid, and the scrotum is only a protective sac holding the testes.

questions.stem: Gametes are made by a type of cell division that halves the chromosome number. Why is this halving essential for sexual reproduction?
options: Two gametes fuse at fertilisation, so halving keeps the chromosome number of each generation constant
It makes the gametes genetically identical to the parent, so the offspring inherit the same traits
It allows the zygote to double its chromosome number each generation as the species evolves
It is the only way a cell can become small enough and light enough to move to the egg
questions.explanation: Each gamete carries one set of chromosomes, so when a sperm and an egg fuse the zygote receives two sets — the normal body-cell number is restored and stays the same generation after generation. The option about doubling each generation reverses the logic: if gametes carried the full number, the chromosome count really would double every generation, which is exactly what halving prevents. Cue: half plus half equals whole, once per generation.

questions.stem: On a few nights each year, corals on a reef all release their eggs and sperm into the water at the same time. What is the main functional advantage of this synchronised mass spawning?
options: It ensures the offspring are genetically identical to the parent colony and therefore well suited to the reef
It lets the eggs develop into new colonies without any sperm, because fertilisation happens later on the seabed
Releasing all gametes together raises the chance that eggs and sperm meet before they are diluted or eaten
It allows each coral to fertilise its own eggs internally, so no other colony is needed
questions.explanation: Corals use external fertilisation, where gametes are quickly dispersed and diluted by currents, so releasing huge numbers simultaneously across the reef greatly increases the chance of successful fusion. The option about identical offspring is tempting because corals can also bud asexually, but spawning involves eggs and sperm from different colonies, so it produces varied offspring. Cue: gametes released into water means external fertilisation, and the challenge is getting them to meet.

questions.stem: Earthworms are hermaphrodites: each worm has both male and female organs. When two worms meet they pair up and exchange sperm rather than fertilising their own eggs. What is the main advantage of this behaviour?
options: The offspring are clones of both parents at once, which preserves two successful sets of traits
Self-fertilisation would produce more variation, so exchanging sperm keeps the offspring uniform
Every worm met is a potential mate, yet the offspring still get genes from two individuals and so vary
Exchanging sperm doubles the chromosome number in the offspring, making them larger and stronger
questions.explanation: Being hermaphrodite solves the problem of finding a mate in soil where encounters are rare, while cross-fertilising rather than self-fertilising keeps two different genomes contributing to each zygote, maintaining variation in the population. The statement that self-fertilisation would give more variation is the reverse of the truth: fertilising your own eggs limits offspring to your own alleles. Cue: two parents means more genetic combinations, whichever organs each parent happens to have.

questions.stem: In the human reproductive system, which pair of organs produces the gametes (sex cells)?
options: The prostate gland in males and the uterus in females
The scrotum in males and the oviducts in females
The vas deferens in males and the cervix in females
The testes in males and the ovaries in females
questions.explanation: Gametes are produced by the gonads: sperm are made in the testes and egg cells mature in the ovaries. The pairing of prostate gland and uterus names two organs that support reproduction (adding fluid to semen, housing the embryo) but neither makes gametes. A useful cue: the gamete-producing organ is always the one the gametes travel away from, not the tube or chamber they travel through.

questions.stem: How do a flower's bright petals and nectaries relate to its function?
options: They protect the developing bud before it opens, then fall away
They receive pollen grains from the air and hold them until fertilisation
They attract insects or birds, which carry pollen between flowers
They produce the pollen grains carried away by visiting insects
questions.explanation: Petals and nectar are advertising and reward: they bring animal visitors into contact with anthers and stigmas so pollen is transferred between plants. Saying they produce the pollen confuses petals with anthers, which are the pollen-producing parts of the stamen. Bud protection is the job of the sepals, and pollen is received by the sticky stigma.

questions.stem: A potato sprouts shoots from its eyes, and each can grow into a new plant. Which is correct?
options: Asexual reproduction, so the new plants show a wide range of variation
Sexual reproduction, because the tuber developed from a fertilised ovule
Asexual reproduction, so the new plants are genetically identical to it
Sexual reproduction, because the eyes contain gametes that fuse together
questions.explanation: A tuber is a swollen underground stem, and growth from its buds involves only ordinary cell division of the parent's cells, so the offspring are clones. The option describing asexual reproduction with wide variation is tempting but self-contradictory: without gametes and fertilisation there is no mixing of genetic material, so variation is almost absent. Remember that a potato tuber is stem tissue, not a seed.

questions.stem: During ejaculation, glands add a fluid containing sugars and salts to the sperm to form semen. How does this relate to the sperm's function?
options: The fluid is where sperm cells are produced before they are released from the penis
The fluid provides a swimming medium and sugars that supply energy for sperm movement
The fluid supplies the sperm with the extra chromosomes needed to fertilise the egg
The fluid dissolves the sperm's tail so it can be absorbed through the uterus wall
questions.explanation: Sperm are stripped-down motile cells with very little stored food, so the seminal fluid transports them and its sugars (such as fructose) fuel the mitochondria that drive the tail. Saying the fluid supplies extra chromosomes is wrong because a sperm already carries its complete single set in its nucleus. Sperm are made in the testes; the glands only add fluid to them.

questions.stem: A single fern plant releases millions of tiny, light, dust-like spores from the underside of its fronds. What is the main survival advantage of this?
options: Each spore carries two sets of chromosomes, so it can grow without needing any water
Spores are formed by the fusion of gametes, so each one is genetically unique
Spores are large food stores, so nearly every one survives and grows into a fern
Huge numbers of easily wind-blown spores mean some will reach suitable damp sites far away
questions.explanation: Spores are a numbers-and-dispersal strategy: most land in unsuitable places, but producing millions of light spores makes it likely that a few reach the moist, shaded conditions ferns need, spreading the species widely. The claim that spores are genetically unique because gametes fused is wrong — spores are made without fertilisation, unlike the fern's later swimming gametes. Note also that a spore is minute and carries almost no food store, which is exactly why so many are made.

questions.stem: A seed contains an embryo, a food store and a tough outer coat. How does this structure relate to the seed's function?
options: The coat absorbs sunlight for the embryo and the food store attracts animals to the seed
The food store contains the male gamete, which fertilises the embryo when the seed germinates
The coat prevents water ever entering, so the embryo can germinate without needing any moisture
The coat protects the embryo while dormant and the food store fuels early growth before leaves form
questions.explanation: A seed must survive a period of dormancy and then support a seedling until it can photosynthesise, so it combines protective coat, embryo and stored food. The idea that the food store contains a male gamete reverses the order of events: fertilisation happened in the flower before the seed formed, so the embryo is already the product of fusion. Also, seeds need to take up water to germinate — the coat resists drying out, it does not exclude water permanently.

questions.stem: What is fertilisation?
options: The fusion of a sperm and an egg
The release of an egg from the ovary
The division of a cell into two
The growth of an embryo in the uterus
questions.explanation: Fertilisation is the moment a sperm and egg fuse, combining their genetic material. Release of the egg is ovulation, which comes first and is the usual mix-up.
questions.teaching:
The sequence matters here, because several of the events in reproduction happen close together and get confused with each other.

Ovulation comes first: an egg is released from an ovary into the oviduct. The event this question asks about happens next, when a sperm nucleus and an egg nucleus join, combining two half-sets of chromosomes into one full set. That single cell then divides repeatedly, and only afterwards does it embed itself in the uterus lining, which is implantation. Three separate steps, in that order — release, joining, embedding — and the question is asking about the middle one.

questions.stem: How many chromosomes does a human body cell have?
questions.explanation: A body cell holds 46 chromosomes, in 23 pairs. 23 is the count in a gamete, which carries one of each pair — that halving is what keeps the number steady from one generation to the next.
questions.teaching:
Chromosomes come in matched pairs in body cells: one of each pair from each parent. Humans have 23 pairs, and the total is simply double that.

The pairing is what makes everything else work. Because each pair has two copies of every gene, you can carry a recessive variant without showing it. And when sex cells are made, the pairs separate so each gamete gets one of each — half the total — which is why fertilisation restores the full number instead of doubling it. So the two figures you need are the pair count and the total, and knowing which is which is what most questions on this actually test.

questions.stem: What is a gamete?
options: Any cell in the body except a sex cell
A cell with two full sets of chromosomes
A fertilised egg before it divides
A sex cell, such as a sperm or an egg
questions.explanation: Gametes are the sex cells, and they carry a single set of chromosomes. A fertilised egg is a zygote, which already has two sets, so it is one step further along.
questions.teaching:
Two cell types are worth separating. Nearly every cell in your body carries a full double set of chromosomes and divides by making identical copies of itself.

A small number do not. These are made by a different kind of division that halves the chromosome number, so they carry a single set rather than a pair of each. That halving is what allows two of them to fuse without doubling the count. In humans they come in two very different forms — one large and packed with food reserves, one tiny and mobile — but both have the same defining feature. Once two have fused, the result is a zygote and already has the full double set again.

questions.stem: Where does a human embryo normally implant?
options: In the wall of the ovary
In the wall of the oviduct itself
In the neck of the cervix
In the lining of the uterus
questions.explanation: The embryo implants in the uterus lining, where the placenta then develops. Implantation in the oviduct does happen and is called an ectopic pregnancy, but it is a medical emergency rather than the normal course.
questions.teaching:
Fertilisation and implantation happen in different places, several days apart, and that gap is what the question is really testing.

An egg is usually fertilised in the oviduct, high up near the ovary. The resulting ball of cells then travels down over roughly a week, dividing as it goes, before embedding itself in the thickened lining prepared for it. The placenta develops from that point of attachment. If the embryo embeds before it completes the journey — in the oviduct itself — the pregnancy cannot continue safely and is called ectopic. That it happens at all is why knowing the normal location matters.

questions.stem: What controls the changes of puberty?
options: Hormones
Enzymes
Antibodies
Neurotransmitters
questions.explanation: Puberty is driven by hormones, chemical messengers carried in the blood from glands to target organs. Enzymes speed up reactions but do not signal between organs, which is the distinction being tested.
questions.teaching:
The body has two communication systems, and they work on very different timescales. Nerves send fast electrical signals for immediate responses. The other system releases chemical messengers into the blood, which act slowly but reach everywhere and keep acting for a long time.

Puberty is unmistakably the second kind: it unfolds over years and changes the whole body at once. The messengers are released by glands — the pituitary in the brain sets the process going, and the ovaries or testes then produce the ones responsible for most of the visible changes. Enzymes are a tempting answer because they are also chemicals, but they speed up reactions rather than carry messages between organs.

questions.stem: What does asexual reproduction produce?
options: Offspring genetically identical to the parent
Offspring carrying genes mixed from two different parents
Offspring with entirely new genes
Offspring that cannot reproduce
questions.explanation: With one parent and no fusion of gametes, the offspring are clones. Mixing genes from two parents is sexual reproduction, and that mixing is the whole source of the variation selection acts on.
questions.teaching:
One parent, no gametes, no fusion — so there is nothing for two sets of genetic material to mix.

The consequence follows directly: the offspring receive a straight copy of the parent's DNA and are genetically identical to it and to each other. Strawberry runners, potato tubers and bacterial division all work this way, and so does taking a cutting. It is fast and needs no mate, which is a real advantage. The cost is that a population produced this way has almost no variation, so a disease or a change in conditions that affects one individual affects all of them equally. Variation is what sexual reproduction buys at the price of needing two parents.

questions.stem: Where are egg cells produced in humans?
options: In the uterus
In the oviducts
In the cervix
In the ovaries
questions.explanation: Eggs are made in the ovaries and released into the oviducts, where fertilisation usually happens. The uterus is where an embryo implants, one step further along.
questions.teaching:
It helps to have the pathway in order, because the organs are named separately and questions often ask which one does what.

Production happens in the paired organs low in the abdomen, which also release the hormones controlling the monthly cycle. From there an egg passes into a tube leading towards the womb, and it is in that tube that fertilisation usually occurs. The womb itself is where an embryo embeds and develops, and its neck is the narrow opening at the lower end. So one organ makes the egg, another carries it, a third houses the pregnancy — and this question is asking about the first.

questions.stem: What is the function of the placenta?
options: Protecting the fetus from every possible infection
Exchanging materials between mother and fetus
Producing the mother's egg cells
Storing the fetus's waste until birth
questions.explanation: The placenta lets oxygen and nutrients pass in and waste pass out, without the two blood supplies mixing. It filters a great deal but not everything, so the total-protection option overstates it.
questions.teaching:
A developing fetus cannot eat, breathe or excrete for itself, so all of that has to happen through the mother — but not by simply plumbing the two bloodstreams together.

The organ that manages it brings the two blood supplies very close without letting them mix, so that oxygen, glucose and antibodies can pass one way and carbon dioxide and waste the other, by diffusion across a thin barrier. Keeping the supplies separate matters, since blood groups may differ and pressures certainly do. The barrier filters a great deal but is not perfect: alcohol, nicotine and some medicines cross it, which is why they are a concern in pregnancy.

questions.stem: What is a zygote?
options: An unfertilised egg
A sperm cell
A fully formed embryo
A fertilised egg cell
questions.explanation: A zygote is the single cell formed the moment sperm and egg fuse, carrying a full set of chromosomes. It divides repeatedly to become an embryo.
questions.teaching:
There is a sequence of names for the earliest stages, and each one marks a specific point, so it is worth having them in order.

Before fertilisation there are two sex cells, each with a single set of chromosomes. The moment they fuse, the result is one cell carrying a full double set — that single cell is the stage this question asks about, and it exists only briefly. It then divides repeatedly, becoming a hollow ball of cells, and once that ball has embedded in the uterus lining it is called an embryo. Later still it is a fetus. So the term here names one cell at one moment, not a stage that lasts.

questions.stem: Which hormone triggers ovulation?
options: Luteinising hormone
Insulin from the pancreas
Adrenaline
Testosterone
questions.explanation: A surge of luteinising hormone causes the ovary to release an egg. Insulin and adrenaline are hormones too, but they regulate glucose and the stress response instead.
questions.teaching:
The menstrual cycle is run by four hormones working in sequence, so questions usually turn on which one does which job.

Two are produced in the ovaries and control the thickening and maintenance of the uterus lining. The other two come from the pituitary gland in the brain: one stimulates an egg to mature, and the other surges sharply about halfway through the cycle to cause its release. It is that surge which ovulation-prediction kits detect. Insulin, adrenaline and testosterone are all real hormones, but they belong to glucose control, the stress response and male development respectively — none of them is part of this cycle.

questions.stem: What is external fertilisation?
options: Reproduction without any gametes
Fertilisation by a single parent
Gametes meeting outside the body
Gametes meeting inside the body
questions.explanation: Many fish and frogs release eggs and sperm into water, where they meet. It needs huge numbers of gametes because so few ever pair up.
questions.teaching:
Fertilisation needs a sperm and an egg to meet, and species solve that problem in two broadly different ways.

Some animals bring the gametes together inside the female's body, which protects them and means far fewer are needed. Others release both into the surrounding water and let chance do the rest — most fish, frogs and corals work this way. The trade-off is stark. The second strategy needs enormous numbers, because gametes are eaten, swept away or simply never meet, and the eggs that are fertilised have no protection afterwards. It also ties the species to water, which is one reason amphibians rarely stray far from it.

questions.stem: Why does meiosis halve the chromosome number?
options: So offspring are identical to parents
So cells can divide more quickly
So mutations are prevented entirely
So fertilisation restores the full set
questions.explanation: Each gamete carries half a set, so fusing two gives a complete set again. Without that halving the number would double every generation.
questions.teaching:
Ask what would happen if it did not. Two parents each contributing a full set would give a child double the number, that child's own children four times, and so on. Within a few generations the arithmetic becomes impossible.

Halving during gamete formation is what prevents it. Each sex cell receives one chromosome from each pair rather than both, so when two gametes fuse the original number is restored exactly. The process also does something else valuable: the pairs are shuffled and swap segments before separating, so no two gametes are alike. That shuffling is a major source of the variation natural selection depends on.
